title: Adaptive Token-Slicing for FlashAttention with Paged KV — sketch notes
content:
Context and goal:

This is a sketch exploring an alternative kernel/scheduling pattern that tries to reduce tail latency and memory stalls for long-context calls when using FlashAttention-style fused attention and a paged KV cache. The idea: dynamically slice tokens across cooperative compute partitions (worker groups) based on on-device memory pressure and per-request token distribution, rather than fixed microbatch sizes or rigid warp-level layouts.

Why this is different from existing notes:
- Focus is on per-request adaptive token slices that interact with paged KV prefetch heuristics (not just static fusion or warp scheduling).
- Emphasis on minimizing synchronous stalls when pages are missing and smoothing compute across concurrent requests by token redistribution.
- Operational, implementation-minded sketches (pseudo-code), heuristics and unresolved tradeoffs — intended as a working doc, not a finalized RFC.

High-level idea:
- Each incoming request is represented as a stream of tokens to be processed (autoregressive or full-attention batch). Instead of committing a fixed microbatch size or fixed tile width per request, the runtime maintains a small pool of "token-slice workers" (logical compute groups).
- Token-slice worker: a cooperative group of warps/threads that processes a contiguous slice of tokens (T_slice) across layers and attends using FlashAttention micro-tiling.
- Token-slices can be resized at layer boundaries; slices for requests with missing KV pages can be shrunk and redistributed to other workers to avoid idle GPU units while I/O completes.

Why this helps with paged KV:
- Paged KV causes intermittent stalls: some requests need to fetch pages (host or remote) while others are ready. Static allocation leaves compute units idle or forces global syncs.
- By making token slices movable and fine-grained, we can continue to process tokens from other requests or different parts of the same request without global pipeline stalls.

Core primitives and invariants:
- WorkerGroup: identifies a GPU cooperative group (e.g., 4 warps) scheduled to run a token slice.
- SliceDescriptor: {request_id, start_token, length, layer_idx, kv_page_bitmap} (store as compact metadata in device-side ring).
- PageState: per-request bitset that tracks which KV pages are resident.
- PrefetchHint: estimated future pages for a slice (generated by runtime heuristics).

Runtime flow (sketch):
1) Incoming requests enqueued with token lengths and initial prefix pages known/resident.
2) Scheduler allocates initial slices to WorkerGroups based on token length distribution and residency. Short requests may be assigned a single slice; long requests broken into many slices spread across groups to improve throughput.
3) WorkerGroup starts FlashAttention kernels for assigned slice. Before each layer, check PageState: if missing page(s), optionally: 
   - shrink current slice (process only resident subrange), publish remaining subrange back to scheduler, and request prefetch for remaining pages; OR
   - if slice too small to be efficient, steal tokens from another ready request's slice (if fair to preempt).
4) When pages arrive, scheduler reassigns pending slices. Slices may be merged (contiguous tokens for same request) to enable larger FlashAttention tile sizes.

Pseudo-code (scheduler side):

// Simplified: assume device-side circular queue of SliceDescriptors for WorkerGroups
function schedule_round():
  ready_slices = pop_ready_slices(max_groups)
  for each slice in ready_slices:
    if not pages_resident(slice):
      if slice.length > min_efficiency_tokens:
        // process resident prefix, split tail for later
        resident_len = resident_prefix_length(slice)
        enqueue_worker(slice.request_id, slice.start, resident_len, slice.layer)
        tail = create_slice(slice.request_id, slice.start + resident_len, slice.length - resident_len, slice.layer)
        pending_slices.push(tail)
        trigger_prefetch(tail)
      else:
        // too small: consider stealing from other ready slice to form efficient tile
        donor = find_donor_slice(ready_slices, min_efficiency_tokens - slice.length)
        if donor:
          steal_tokens = min(donor.length - min_efficiency_tokens, min_efficiency_tokens - slice.length)
          adjust_slices(donor, slice, steal_tokens)
        else:
          trigger_prefetch(slice);
    else:
      assign_worker(slice)

Kernel-level sketch (device):
- Each WorkerGroup reads SliceDescriptor; performs a small resident-page mask check.
- Use FlashAttention micro-tiling: inner loop loads Q/K/V tiles sized to L1-friendly footprint; reuse L2/GEMM if available.
- If page boundary hit while streaming KV, complete current microtile, write partial KV to device ring and exit kernel cooperatively (no fatal error). This enables kernel to yield without full block sync.

Micro-tiling heuristics:
- Tile width should be a function of: warp_coop_factor, expected KV locality (pages per token), and per-layer sequence length. Experiment: target ~32–128 tokens per microtile for most A100-class L2 behavior.
- When KV pages are entirely resident for a slice: merge adjacent slices to form larger attention tiles (amortize kernel launch overhead).

Prefetch heuristics (interaction with scheduler):
- Conservative mode: prefetch only pages predicted by immediate next N layers for the current active slice. Lower IO spikes, higher latency for misses.
- Aggressive mode: prefetch pages for predicted next-M tokens across multiple requests if free bandwidth. Lower tail latency but risks wasting host memory/bandwidth.
- Adaptive mode (recommended): track per-request miss rate and host fetch latency; increase prefetch window for requests with low miss penalties and decrease for high-latency sources (S3 vs local NVMe).

Latency vs throughput tradeoffs:
- Small slices reduce blocking and tail latency for page misses but increase kernel launch overhead and reduce arithmetic intensity.
- Larger slices increase efficiency but increase the cost of a page miss (larger chunk stalled). The scheduler must find the sweet spot; start with target slice size based on recent effective throughput and adjust with an online control loop.

Safety and fairness:
- Need fairness constraints: limit the number of slices any single request can occupy concurrently to avoid starve-other-requests scenarios.
- Backpressure signals to the prefetcher and network stack when device-side pending pages exceed threshold.

Unresolved engineering details / TODOs:
- Device-resident SliceDescriptor queue layout (compact, atomic update pattern). How to do low-overhead enqueue/steal?
- How to safely merge slices on-device without heavy synchronization? Possible approach: epoch counters + compare-and-swap on slice headers.
- Kernel cooperative exit on page boundary: experiment with returning control to scheduler via lightweight stream callback vs launching next kernel for remainder.
- Exact microtile sizes: run microbench matrix across batch sizes 1-64, seq lengths 128..8192 on A100/RTX8000.
- Prefetch cost model: build simple online estimator for host fetch latency and miss probability by page age and request fingerprint.

Quick experiments to run (practical):
- Synthetic workload with mixed short(<=64), medium(512), long(2048-8192) requests; paged KV misses randomly distributed; measure p50/p95/p99 latency and GPU utilization under: fixed-slice (baseline), adaptive-token-slicing (this doc), and donor-steal disabled/enabled.
- Microbenchmark FlashAttention microtile sizes and kernel occupancy across slice widths.
- Measure prefetch bandwidth utilization under conservative/aggressive/adaptive modes.

Notes to self / implementation checklist:
- Prototype scheduler in Python inside the runtime simulator first (no CUDA) to validate slice redistribution logic.
- Add lightweight metrics: slice_size_hist, page_miss_per_slice, steal_events, slice_merge_events.
- Implement device-side bitmap for page residency (sparse, compressed) and benchmark query cost.
- Draft minimal CUDA kernel that supports partial return on page miss (cooperative_kill_path) and measure overhead.

References and related tickets:
- Related PRs: serving-runtime#1842 (paged-kv prefetch optimizations), kernel-lab#627 (flashattn micro-tiling experiments).
- Jira: JIRA-RT-1123 (paged-kv staging policy), JIRA-RT-1188 (streaming attention regressions).
- Slack: internal thread discussing host->device NVMe prefetch limits (thread link above).

Open questions for review:
- Is device-side stealing too complex? Could we prefer scheduler-driven steals only to keep device kernels simple?
- How does this interact with multi-tenant dedicated capacity with strong isolation requirements? If a tenant owns GPU, stealing across tenants is not allowed; we should scope stealing inside tenant boundaries.
- What are worst-case memory amplification effects if aggressive prefetch overlaps across many requests? Add guardrails by host memory budget per-tenant.

Summary:
Adaptive token-slicing is a middle-ground between coarse microbatch strategies and per-warp rigid layouts. It aims to reduce tail stalls introduced by paged KV by allowing dynamic redistribution of token work and smarter prefetching. This doc captures the sketch and immediate experiment plan. If the results look promising in the simulator, follow-up: prototype minimal device-side support for cooperative exit + runtime slice queue and benchmark on A100.

Immediate next step: Marcus to produce a small runtime simulator (Python) that models slices, page residency and prefetch latencies; Priya to define a baseline microtile benchmark matrix; I'll prototype a trimmed CUDA kernel for partial-exit behavior (if we decide to go device-steal route).

-- end of notes --
